summary: A US jury convicts Huawei, Russia warns Estonia of "open war", a report says Moscow may put a nuclear weapon in orbit, Solomon Islands drops a China pact, and Iran sets terms for talks.

question.text: Estonia is closing its border to stop sabotage, and Solomon Islands is leaving a security pact in exchange for closer ties with Australia. For each decision, what might it change two or three steps later, for ordinary people on both sides, that the leaders making it may not intend?

read.title: What the ICJ genocide ruling means for the Rohingya people
read.summary: An explainer on last week's first-ever World Court finding that a state committed genocide: what the judges found, what Myanmar must now do, and why enforcing it is hard.

topics.heading: A US jury convicts Huawei of fraud and trade-secret theft but clears it of racketeering
topics.summary: A federal jury in Brooklyn found Huawei and three affiliates guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets.[^1] It acquitted the company of racketeering conspiracy and obstruction, and Huawei says it will appeal.[^1]

lead.title: Huawei convicted in US as Chinese tech giant emerges as Nvidia rival

alsoReported.title: In closings, Chinese tech giant Huawei is cast by prosecutors as a villain as its lawyer disagrees

article: Huawei is the world's largest maker of the equipment that runs mobile phone networks, and in recent years it has also become China's leading designer of AI chips.[^2][^1] On Tuesday a US federal jury in Brooklyn, New York, found the company and three affiliates guilty on 10 of 12 criminal counts after a trial of more than two months. The counts included bank fraud, wire fraud, breaking US sanctions and conspiring to steal trade secrets.[^1]

The jury did not accept the most sweeping charge. It acquitted Huawei of racketeering conspiracy, a law usually used against organized crime, and of obstruction of justice.[^1] Huawei's lawyer says the company will appeal and argues that the racketeering acquittal weakens the government's whole case.[^1]

Prosecutors said Huawei's leaders set a tone of lying to banks and Congress, and that employees took technology from US firms, including router code allegedly copied from Cisco.[^1] In closing arguments last week, the defence said prosecutors started from guilt and worked backwards, that the wrongdoing came from a few employees who were fired, and that some of the information was already public.[^2] Chinese officials have long called the US case "economic bullying" that uses national security as a pretext.[^2]

Some background: Canada arrested Huawei's finance chief, Meng Wanzhou, in 2018 on a US warrant tied to this case. She returned to China in 2021 under a deal with prosecutors, and the charges against her were later dropped.[^1] Huawei has been barred from selling to US carriers and was put on a US trade blacklist in 2019. Canada and Britain have also blocked its equipment.[^2][^1]

What next: the company could face penalties worth billions of dollars, though Newsweek notes the money may matter less to a firm already largely shut out of the US.[^1] My read: the verdict will be read in Beijing and Washington as part of the wider contest over chips and AI, arriving in the same week as the Nvidia leadership drama.
topics.differences: Prosecutors describe a company-wide culture of theft and fraud; Huawei says a few fired employees were to blame and that it will appeal; Chinese officials call the prosecution politically motivated.[^1][^2]

topics.heading: Russia says Estonia is near "open war" as Tallinn prepares to shut its border
topics.summary: Russia's foreign ministry summoned Estonia's top diplomat in Moscow and said Tallinn's "hostile actions" are on the verge of triggering open war.[^3][^4] Estonia rejects the accusations and still plans to close its border crossings with Russia from Dec 1.[^3]

alsoReported.title: Moscow Summons Estonian Diplomat Over Border Closure

article: Estonia, a small NATO and EU member, shares a land border with Russia. Last week it said it would close its last three road crossings, at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula, from Dec 1 for at least six months.[^5][^4] It made the decision after its security services said they foiled an arson attack on a local drone maker, which Estonia blames on Russian military intelligence. Eight suspects living in Latvia were arrested.[^5] Russia denies involvement.[^3]

On Monday Russia's foreign ministry summoned Estonia's chargé d'affaires in Moscow to protest. It accused Estonia of quietly letting Ukrainian drones cross its airspace to attack northwest Russia, blocking Russian cargo ships in the Baltic, and mistreating Russian speakers and the Orthodox Church. It said these actions bring the two countries "to the brink of an open war", and that it reserves the right to take political and diplomatic steps.[^4][^3]

Estonia's foreign ministry said it does not engage with Russian "propaganda narratives" and has never let another country use its territory for military operations.[^3] Kyiv says drones that stray into Baltic airspace are knocked off course by Russian signal jamming.[^3] NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the alliance is watching Estonia and the recent missile incursion into Poland, and has options to respond.[^3]

Why it matters: Al Jazeera notes that Russia justified its 2014 moves into eastern Ukraine partly with claims about protecting Russian speakers, which is one reason such language worries Baltic governments.[^3] This is a judgment, but strong words from Moscow do not by themselves signal an attack; the more concrete tests are what happens at the border after Dec 1 and whether sabotage incidents continue.
topics.differences: Russia says Estonia lets Ukrainian drones use its airspace and persecutes Russian speakers; Estonia denies this. Estonia says Russian intelligence was behind the arson plot; Russia denies it.[^3][^4][^5]

topics.heading: German media say Russia may soon launch a nuclear-armed satellite; the Kremlin scoffs
topics.summary: A joint investigation by German broadcasters and a newspaper reports that Western intelligence expects Russia to launch a nuclear-armed satellite as early as December.[^6] The Kremlin says the report is hardly worth taking seriously.[^7][^6]

lead.title: Kremlin Dismisses Reports About Alleged Nuclear-Armed Satellite Launch

alsoReported.title: Kremlin dismisses German reports about alleged Russian nuclear-armed satellite launch

article: Satellites carry phone signals, navigation, weather data and internet links for ordinary life on the ground. A nuclear weapon in orbit worries governments because it would not need to hit satellites directly: the US Defense Intelligence Agency has warned such a system could degrade thousands of them at once.[^6]

On Monday a joint investigation by the German public broadcasters WDR and NDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that intelligence shared among NATO members says Russia could launch such a satellite, called "Sputnik-S", as soon as December. According to the report, the satellite was built years ago and stored near Moscow.[^6] The claim rests on unnamed intelligence sources; no government has confirmed it on the record.[^6]

The Kremlin's spokesman said he had not seen the report and that claims full of "alleged" and "possible" were hardly worth taking seriously.[^7] Russia's embassy in Berlin called it part of a propaganda campaign and said Russia's space activities are peaceful.[^6]

There is earlier context. In February 2024 the White House said Russia was pursuing a "troubling" anti-satellite capability, and in October 2026 the DIA said Russia is developing a nuclear-armed satellite, which would break the 1967 Outer Space Treaty banning nuclear weapons in orbit.[^6] Russia has called those claims unfounded.[^6]

How do we know? For now, we don't. The honest summary is that several Western agencies have been warning about this for years, the timing in this report is new, and Russia denies it. A launch itself would be visible to tracking networks, so this is a claim that can be checked in the coming weeks.
topics.differences: Western intelligence, as reported by German media and earlier US agencies, says Russia is building a nuclear-armed satellite; the Kremlin and Russia's embassy call the reports unfounded propaganda.[^6][^7]

topics.heading: Solomon Islands tells China it will not renew their 2022 security pact
topics.summary: Solomon Islands has told Beijing it will let a 2022 security agreement lapse when it ends in April 2027, ABC News reports, as Prime Minister Matthew Wale visits Canberra to sign a treaty with Australia.[^8] China says it does not engage in "bloc confrontation".[^8]

lead.title: Solomons Islands scraps China security pact in 'massive win' for Australia

article: Solomon Islands is a Pacific island nation north-east of Australia. In 2022 its then-government signed a secret security pact with China that lets Chinese police training teams rotate through the country; about two dozen Chinese police are there at any time.[^8] Australia and the US worried the deal could one day lead to a Chinese military presence close to Australia.

ABC News, citing sources, confirms that the new government of Prime Minister Matthew Wale, in office since May, has told Beijing it will not renew the pact when its five-year term ends in April 2027.[^8] Wale arrived in Canberra on Tuesday, and a new treaty with Australia was due to be signed on Wednesday. Its full terms have not been released.[^8] ABC earlier reported that Australia would provide about $980 million in extra funding.[^8]

Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong once called the 2022 deal Australia's worst foreign policy blunder in the Pacific since the Second World War.[^8] China's foreign ministry said it builds ties "on the principle of equality" and does not take part in geopolitical contests.[^8]

Not everyone in Solomon Islands agrees. Former prime minister Manasseh Sogavare, who signed the China pact, warned about what the country could lose, and the opposition accuses Australia of "chequebook diplomacy".[^8] A Lowy Institute analyst called it a "massive win" for Australia but asked what was offered in return.[^8]

My read: small Pacific states are choosing among larger partners for money and security, and they can switch. Watch whether the treaty text is published and whether Wale, who has already faced one no-confidence vote, keeps his majority.
topics.differences: Australia and supporters see a win for regional security; Sogavare and the opposition see a costly swap bought with Australian money; China says it does not compete for blocs.[^8]

topics.heading: Iran sets seven conditions for talks as the US probes cyberattacks on up to 50 ships
topics.summary: Iran's chief negotiator says there will be no talks with the US until seven conditions, including lifting the naval blockade, are met.[^10] US investigators are looking at whether Iran was behind cyberattacks on as many as 50 commercial ships, while Qatar keeps trying to mediate.[^9][^11]

lead.title: Live Updates: Iran says it will use all means to end U.S. blockade as Trump plays down escalating attacks

alsoReported.title: Middle East conflict: Iran warns Hormuz ships, rules out US talks until 7 conditions met

article: The US keeps a naval blockade on Iranian ports, and Iran has tried to control traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel that carries much of the world's oil.[^9] On Monday Iran's foreign ministry called the blockade "an act of military aggression" and said Iran will use all available means to end it.[^9]

Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who leads Iran's negotiators, said Iran will not talk to the US until seven conditions are met. Gulf News reports they include lifting the blockade, easing sanctions, releasing frozen funds and declaring the war over.[^10] Iran's navy said three tankers hit mines in the strait on Monday; that is Iran's claim. UK maritime authorities confirmed an attack on one tanker anchored off the UAE, with a fire but no reported casualties.[^9]

A new front is digital. The Wall Street Journal reported that US investigators are examining cyberattacks on up to 50 ships carrying oil, gas and chemicals, with Iran the main suspect and Russia also considered; responsibility has not been established.[^9][^10] Meanwhile Qatar's prime minister met Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington and says Qatar is working with both sides because the region "cannot withstand further escalation".[^11]

Pressure is visible inside Iran. After new US sanctions on its shadow-banking network, the rial fell about 5% on the black market, to around 2.82 million per US dollar, according to Gulf News.[^10] Oil prices have eased, with Brent near $88 a barrel.[^10]

My read: both sides are setting public terms while letting Qatar carry messages. The conditions Iran lists are close to what it has demanded before, so a quick deal looks unlikely; the risk is that a disputed incident at sea, or a cyberattack blamed on one side, pushes events faster than diplomacy.
topics.differences: Iran calls the blockade aggression and blames the US for the escalation; President Trump says Iran's recent drones and missiles did no damage and that Iran breaks deals.[^9] US officials say Iran's economy is near collapse; Iran's officials reject that.[^10]
